Reading the gallery

Three things these images should tell you

Aesthetics matter less than the decisions behind them — but the decisions are visible if you know where to look.

Layout follows the roof, not a template

Arrays are shaped around vents, valleys and shading rather than forced into a rectangle. A neat layout is usually easier to service and less likely to be compromised by a late change.

Storage placement is a design decision

Battery location affects temperature, ventilation, cable runs and clearance compliance. A garage wall beside the switchboard is common for good reasons — but it is not the only option.

The electrical work is the invisible half

Switchboard capacity, protection and isolation are what make the rest safe. It is the least photogenic part of an installation and the part that is hardest to fix later.

Component glossary

The parts behind the pictures.

Captions name components; this is what each one actually does — useful when two quotes disagree about specifications, and when they agree on price.

Solar module (the panel)

Converts sunlight into DC electricity. Wattage, cell technology and build quality vary between modules, and total system output depends on all of them — plus layout, orientation and how the inverter is matched.

Mounting system

Rails, clamps, roof hooks or ballast. This is what holds the array against wind and weather; how roof penetrations are flashed and sealed is decided here, and it is among the least visible quality differences between quotes.

Inverter

Converts panel DC into household AC. String, hybrid or micro-inverter — and in a hybrid, the unit that couples array, battery and grid. It is usually the first major component to need attention or replacement.

Battery

Stores energy for later use. Capacity in kilowatt hours says how much it can hold; power in kilowatts says how fast it can deliver. Two different numbers — a large battery with modest power may not run the appliances you have in mind.

Switchboard

The building's distribution point. Circuit capacity, protection devices, isolation and the new solar circuits all land here. The state and age of the switchboard constrains what can be installed before anything reaches the roof.

Metering

Measures electricity imported from and exported to the grid. A smart meter configured for solar is what makes exports visible, enables time-of-use decisions and keeps billing accurate.

Monitoring

The reporting layer: generation, consumption and battery flows over time. It is both a reassurance tool and the first diagnostic when something changes — which is why a system without working monitoring is only half installed.

System design and approvals

Layout drawings, string plans, network applications and compliance documentation. On a solar job, "planning" means design and connection approval — not town planning — and it happens before anyone books an installation date.
